title: The Day of Egypt and Pharaoh's Broken Arms
summary: Ezekiel announces that the Day of the LORD is near for Egypt: a sword will fall on the land and its allies, Nebuchadnezzar will be the instrument, and one by one Egypt's great cities, from Memphis to Thebes, will burn. In a dated oracle God says he has already broken one of Pharaoh's arms and will break the other, while he strengthens the arms of the king of Babylon and places his own sword in his hand.
story: Chapter 30 continues the oracles against Egypt begun in chapter 29. Where the previous chapter focused on Pharaoh's pride and Egypt's betrayal of Israel, this one describes the judgment itself, first as a sweeping Day of the LORD across the whole land (verses 1 to 19), then as a specific event already under way (verses 20 to 26). For the exiles, still waiting for news of Jerusalem, the message was pointed. The power Zedekiah had trusted to break the siege had already been broken, and there was no rescue coming from the south. The chapter keeps pressing the book's central lesson: God, not Egypt or Babylon, controls the fate of nations.
historical:
The first oracle (verses 1 to 19) is undated. The second (verses 20 to 26) is dated to the eleventh year, first month, seventh day, in the spring of 587 BC, a few months after the oracle of 29:1. The broken arm of verse 21 is almost certainly the failure of Pharaoh Hophra's army, which marched toward Jerusalem during the siege and then withdrew when the Babylonians moved against it (Jeremiah 37:5-11). Hophra's reign ended badly: according to the Greek historian Herodotus, he was overthrown by one of his own officers, Amasis, around 570 BC, after a military disaster.

The cities named in verses 13 to 18 cover Egypt from north to south. Memphis (Noph) was the ancient capital near modern Cairo. Zoan, called Tanis by the Greeks, and Pi-beseth, known as Bubastis, lay in the eastern Nile Delta. On was Heliopolis, center of the sun cult. Pelusium (Sin) guarded the eastern frontier on the road from Canaan. Tahpanhes, also in the eastern Delta, is where Jeremiah and a group of Judean refugees fled after Jerusalem's fall (Jeremiah 43:7-9). Thebes (No) was the great religious capital of Upper Egypt, and Pathros was Upper Egypt itself. Cush, Put, and Lud (verse 5) were peoples of Nubia, Libya, and possibly western Anatolia or Africa whose soldiers served as Egyptian allies or mercenaries.
cultural:
The Day of the LORD was a phrase Israel's prophets used for the time when God would act decisively in judgment. Earlier prophets had turned it against Israel itself (Amos 5:18-20; Zephaniah 1:14-16, which also calls it a day of clouds). Ezekiel here turns it against Egypt, as Isaiah and Jeremiah had done for other nations. The phrase does not always mean the end of the world; it means the day when God's rule breaks into history.

The image of Pharaoh's arm carried special force. Egyptian kings were commonly portrayed with a raised arm striking down enemies, and the strong arm was a standard royal symbol of power in Egypt. Israel's own memory of the exodus used the same image in reverse: the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm (Deuteronomy 5:15). To break Pharaoh's arms, both of them, and put God's sword in the hand of Babylon's king, was to say that the power that once enslaved Israel had been disarmed by the God of the exodus.
literary: The chapter has two oracles. The first is a poem of judgment in several stanzas, each introduced by this is what the Lord GOD says (verses 2, 6, 10, and 13). It opens with a call to wail, moves from the general Day of the LORD to the nations allied with Egypt, names Nebuchadnezzar as the agent, and ends with a rapid list of Egyptian cities, each paired with a verb of destruction: lay waste, set fire, execute judgment, pour out wrath. The effect is of a fire moving from city to city. The second oracle is a prose piece built on a single image, the arm, repeated six times. Pharaoh's arms are broken and fall limp; Babylon's are strengthened. The recognition formula, they will know that I am the LORD, closes both halves.

outline.t: Wail: the Day of the LORD is near for Egypt
Egypt's allies fall; terror in Cush
Judgment on the cities of Egypt

doctrines.note: The Day of the LORD falls on Egypt, its allies, its idols, and its cities. Judgment reaches not only rulers but the whole system of power and worship that supported them.
God says he will place his sword in the hand of Babylon's king (verses 24 and 25). The rise and fall of empires is presented as God strengthening one arm and breaking another.

God will destroy the idols and images of Memphis (verse 13). The judgment on Egypt is also a judgment on its gods, echoing the exodus, when God executed judgment on all the gods of Egypt (Exodus 12:12).

words.note: Yom, day, used seven times here. The chapter speaks of the Day of the LORD, that day, and the day of Egypt's doom. In the prophets a day can mean a decisive time of God's action rather than a single twenty-four-hour period.

Zeroa, arm, a symbol of strength and power in action. The arm of Pharaoh, the proud emblem of Egyptian kingship, is broken, while the arms of Babylon's king are strengthened. Israel knew the LORD as the God of the outstretched arm.

Shavar, to break or shatter. It is used for breaking Pharaoh's arms, breaking the yoke of Egypt (verse 18), and shattering Egypt's helpers (verse 8). The word underlines that Egypt's strength will not be merely weakened but broken.

christ: The Day of the LORD, announced here against Egypt, is a thread the New Testament takes up and applies to the return of Christ and the final judgment (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10). The prophets used the phrase for many days of God's intervention in history, and the New Testament sees them as foreshadowings of a final day. The chapter's picture of God breaking the arm of the oppressor also belongs to the exodus pattern that the New Testament applies to Christ's victory. Mary sings that God has shown strength with his arm and brought down rulers from their thrones (Luke 1:51-52), and Paul describes Christ disarming the powers and authorities through the cross (Colossians 2:15). The link is one of pattern and theme: the God who broke Pharaoh's arm is the God who overcomes every power that holds people captive.
questions: Egypt's allies and mercenaries fell with it. What happens to those who tie their security to a power that is about to fall?
God broke Pharaoh's arm and strengthened Babylon's, yet Babylon too would later be judged. How does this shape the way you view the rise and fall of nations in your own lifetime?
Israel remembered God as the one who saved with an outstretched arm. Where have you seen God's strength at work when your own was broken?
